analysis.one_liner: Establishes a publicly funded national health insurance covering every U.S. resident for health and long-term care.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced April 5, 1993 with no cosponsors, was referred to seven House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have guaranteed every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident a covered package of health care and long-term care, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health plans with a single system run by a new Federal Health Board and nonprofit state agencies. It would have been financed by progressive premiums on individuals and employers, with hospitals paid through negotiated global budgets and providers paid negotiated fee schedules. It never got a hearing vote or a floor vote: after referral to seven committees and several subcommittees, no further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, all U.S. residents would gain comprehensive coverage with no deductibles, no cost-sharing on preventive care, and no lifetime or scope limits beyond what the bill itself allows; people with employer coverage would gain portability and protection from medical bills, and families facing long-term care costs would gain income and spousal protections. Rural and underserved areas would gain expanded community health services and training funding directed toward primary care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident needing health coverage

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien to covered health care and long-term care services, with automatic enrollment and a portable state health insurance card.

Covers hospital care, physician and dental services, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive care with no cost-sharing, hospice, rehabilitation, and approved experimental treatment, and bars states from imposing deductibles or limiting covered services.
Repeals Medicare and Medicaid and folds federal employee and military health benefits into the new program, ending the patchwork of separate programs.

Finances the program with progressive, income-based premiums from individuals and employers, dedicates the revenue to a Federal Health Care Trust Fund, and makes provider payment payment-in-full so individuals owe nothing beyond set copayments.
Directs at least half of graduate medical education funding to primary care training and expands the National Health Service Corps and community health centers in medically underserved areas.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and employers would pay new income-based premiums, and employers would pay contributions scaled to workforce size and profitability, with the option of covering their employees' share. States would fund the remainder (roughly 15-25% of program costs) from taxes. Private insurers would lose the main employer-based market, though supplemental and duplicative private coverage would remain allowed, and providers would face negotiated global budgets and fee schedules instead of open billing.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a powerful nine-member Federal Health Board, appointed by the President and insulated from removal, whose budget, premium, and coverage decisions take effect automatically unless both houses of Congress pass a disapproval resolution within 60 days, shifting major spending and coverage decisions out of regular legislation.

Provider payment would be set through state-negotiated fee schedules and fixed hospital budgets, which hospitals and physician groups could be expected to argue would constrain revenue and reduce flexibility compared with fee-for-service payment.

The financing design is complex: states must raise their own shares on top of federal transfers, the new premium mechanism replaces Medicare payroll financing, and existing child health tax credits are phased out, leaving transition costs and administrative burden on states and households.

Private insurance is not abolished: the bill explicitly allows supplemental coverage and even duplicative coverage for services the public program covers, which the bill itself directs the Priorities Council to study for effects on cost and quality.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver the largest single expansion of coverage in American history, replacing premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket cost exposure with a progressive tax-based system, and its no-deductible, no-limit benefit design directly protects people from medical bankruptcy. The tradeoffs are real but ordinary for single-payer designs: a large new tax burden on households and employers, a shift of power from insurers and providers to government boards, and a governance structure (an insulated Federal Health Board whose decisions become law unless Congress actively disapproves) that trades accountability for speed. The bill's allowance of duplicative private insurance would blunt some of its administrative-savings goals. On balance it is a well-developed version of a national health insurance model, not a badly designed one, but its scale means the transition risks — to state budgets, providers, and the financing base — are substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to seven House committees and then to several subcommittees, and sat there without a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas H. Andrews of Maine introduced the National Health Security Act of 1993 on April 5, 1993, to provide universal access to basic health care and long-term care services.
The bill was referred to seven House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Rules, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, and Post Office and Civil Service.
In April 1993 it was sent to multiple subcommittees, including the Subcommittee on Health, and executive comment was requested from the Department of Defense; no committee or floor action followed.
The Congress ended January 3, 1995, with the bill never reported out of committee and never voted on in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept the employer-based market intact, and employers faced no new premium obligations. The roughly 40 million uninsured Americans of the era remained without coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the uninsured stayed where they were

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 5, 1993 and delivered introductory remarks; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House committees of referral (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Rules, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Post Office and Civil Service)
against.role: Committees to which the bill was jointly referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; it was sent to subcommittees in April 1993 and was never reported out for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes recorded, the record shows no measurable partisan lineup on the bill itself, though universal-coverage fights of the 103rd Congress broadly split along party lines.

industries.note: The bill repeals the private employer-based and Medicare/Medicaid financing structure and replaces it with a public plan, eliminating the core market for private major-medical insurance; only supplemental and limited duplicative coverage would remain, and employer deductions for group health plans would exist only for the public program.

They would gain universal coverage eliminating uncompensated care, but lose pricing power: operating, capital, and training costs would be paid through state-negotiated global budgets rather than billed per service.
Guaranteed payment with no patient bad debt, but fee schedules negotiated by state boards would cap income, and mandatory assignment means no balance billing above the negotiated rate.

A new entitlement to nursing home, home- and community-based, and hospice care would create a large, reliable payer for long-term care services that Medicare largely does not cover, with income protections for patients.
